reference.source: Goldfrank's Toxicologic Emergencies / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: A potentially fatal toxic reaction to chloramphenicol occurring predominantly in neonates, especially preterm infants
Features develop over hours to days and include vomiting, poor feeding, abdominal distension, hypothermia and a characteristic ashen-grey skin colour
Progresses to hypotension, cyanosis, cardiovascular collapse and metabolic acidosis
The syndrome results from accumulation of chloramphenicol due to immature hepatic glucuronidation and reduced renal excretion in the newborn
Prevention relies on avoiding chloramphenicol where possible in neonates and, when unavoidable, using reduced dosing with drug-level monitoring
Management is immediate cessation of the drug and aggressive supportive care of the circulation and acidosis
Extracorporeal removal (for example haemoperfusion or exchange transfusion) may be considered in severe accumulation
Older children and adults can also develop toxicity if hepatic metabolism is overwhelmed by excessive dosing
reference.pathophysiology: Chloramphenicol is normally inactivated by hepatic conjugation with glucuronic acid and the conjugate is excreted renally. Neonates, particularly premature infants, have immature UDP-glucuronosyltransferase activity and reduced glomerular filtration, so unconjugated drug accumulates to toxic concentrations. High levels impair mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and electron transport, reducing cellular energy production, especially in the myocardium and vasculature. The result is myocardial depression, loss of vascular tone, hypotension, tissue hypoxia and lactic (metabolic) acidosis, producing the grey, cyanotic, hypotensive infant. The syndrome is therefore a pharmacokinetic accumulation phenomenon rather than an idiosyncratic or immune reaction.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital cardiac disease with circulatory collapse
Inborn errors of metabolism presenting with acidosis
Other drug toxicities in the neonate
additionalInvestigations: Chloramphenicol serum concentration and therapeutic drug monitoring
Arterial blood gas for metabolic acidosis and lactate
Full blood count (chloramphenicol also causes marrow suppression)
Blood cultures and septic screen to exclude infection
redFlags: Ashen-grey skin with hypotension and poor perfusion
Progressive metabolic acidosis and rising lactate
reference.prognosis: The syndrome carries a high mortality once cardiovascular collapse is established, but early recognition, drug withdrawal and supportive care improve survival. Prevention through cautious neonatal use and monitoring is far more effective than treatment.
pitfalls: Using standard weight-based dosing without accounting for immature neonatal metabolism
Attributing the deterioration to sepsis alone and continuing the drug
Failing to monitor chloramphenicol levels when its use is unavoidable
Overlooking the concurrent risk of dose-related bone marrow suppression
management: Stop chloramphenicol immediately, as the syndrome results from toxic drug accumulation
Support the failing circulation with fluid resuscitation and inotropic or vasopressor agents for hypotension and cardiovascular collapse
Correct the metabolic (lactic) acidosis and provide oxygen and ventilatory support as needed
Consider enhanced elimination with exchange transfusion or charcoal haemoperfusion to remove drug in severe toxicity
Monitor serum chloramphenicol concentrations, arterial blood gases and lactate, and the full blood count for accompanying marrow suppression, with continuous cardiovascular monitoring
Prevent recurrence by avoiding chloramphenicol in neonates where possible and, when unavoidable, using reduced dosing with therapeutic drug monitoring
Manage in a neonatal intensive care setting
